facts.statement: Whether the new 404 is an intended API correction or a regression in supported route syntax remains unknown.
The behavior change is linked to 0.13.5 escaping regex metacharacters in route path strings.
PR 1010 proposes special-casing a final question mark and adds tests for both slash variants.
Restoring optional trailing-slash behavior by treating a final question mark as raw route regex is not the accepted API direction.
One canonical slash form plus automatic redirect is the maintainer's initial supported alternative.
The compatibility impact also reaches a wildcard SPA route written as /.*, not only the root /? form.
Route and Mount path strings expose URI templating, not arbitrary embedded regular expressions.
A path converter is the supported alternative for the wildcard-segment use case.
A 307 redirect is not behaviorally equivalent for every caller because it can lose CORS headers and adds a redirect round trip.
Whether to revert and later reapply the escaping change with a larger release and clearer documentation remains undecided.
The wildcard-route reporter confirms that the supported path-converter alternative works for the SPA case.
Registering both slash and no-slash route forms directly avoids raw regex and a redirect for the root endpoint.
How TestClient should activate application lifespan for request tests is still unknown.
Async resources used by the app must be initialized on the same event loop as the TestClient application.
A manual blocking-portal lifespan dispatch is the current prototype under investigation.
Use TestClient as a context manager to activate startup and shutdown.
Adding manual lifespan dispatch to TestClient internals is unnecessary for this use case.
The reported lifespan need is resolved by existing behavior rather than a new patch.
Whether StaticFiles should follow symlinks remains open.
The first pull request attempts support for following symlinks outside the static directory.
Maintainers currently consider the symlink request fixed by the first merged change.
The first merged fix was reverted, so its resolved status is no longer valid.
A safe replacement for the reverted symlink behavior is unresolved.
A second pull request is the active implementation attempt after the revert.
The design must not make exposure through user-controlled symlinks an implicit default.
The preferred boundary is an explicit follow_symlink option whose default is false.
Reviewers still require a risk and alternatives justification before accepting the second attempt.
Restoring unconditional external symlink following is rejected for this redesign.
On the reported RHEL 8 FIPS system, Starlette 0.16.0 FileResponse ETag construction raises ValueError from hashlib.md5.
The reviewable narrow path is a usedforsecurity compatibility change; replacing the hash algorithm remains a separate design discussion.
Requiring a security-grade hash for this ETag is withdrawn; the compatibility problem can be addressed while retaining MD5.
Use a compatibility wrapper that can call hashlib.md5 with usedforsecurity=False rather than assuming ordinary MD5 calls work under FIPS.
PR 1366 opens a compatibility-helper implementation without adding a repository test file in its initial patch.
Issue 1365 is tracker-closed when PR 1366 merges, but that state does not itself verify FIPS behavior.
RHEL backports make runtime capability different from a simple upstream Python-version boundary, so compatibility needs probing rather than version inference.
Whether the first merged wrapper actually works on the target FIPS setup remains to be tested rather than inferred from try/except.
Target FIPS verification is still unavailable because the customer temporarily disabled FIPS mode.
The first merged implementation fails a real FIPS import because its capability probe passes usedforsecurity=True and triggers ValueError.
Treating PR 1366 merge or the first tracker close as proof that FIPS behavior works is invalidated by the later target-system failure.
The follow-up should preserve parameter detection while changing the capability probe itself to usedforsecurity=False.
Issue 1365 is reopened after the first accepted direction fails on the reported FIPS path.
PR 1410 changes the compatibility probe in _compat.py and adds no repository regression test.
The reporter observes the revised probe working on one FIPS system, but cannot verify current master because of a FastAPI compatibility limit.
Issue 1365 closes when PR 1410 merges; this is repository and tracker acceptance, not proof for every Python, OpenSSL, or FIPS combination.
Current master and cross-environment FIPS behavior remain unverified; PR 1410 has no repository test and the reporter could not test current master.
Calling request.form() in BaseHTTPMiddleware and then again in the endpoint reproduces a blocking request.
Middleware and routing construct different Request paths over the same receive channel, so a cache local to one Request does not automatically reach the next Request.
PR 500 proposes storing body bytes in the ASGI scope and tests reading them from a newly constructed Request.
The broad PR 500 scope-cache direction is punted and closes unmerged because its behavior for streamed request bodies is not defined.
Request data consumed as a stream may be irreversibly unavailable downstream; any buffered-body solution must preserve that streaming boundary.
Request.body() and json() can reuse cached bytes, while form() consumes the underlying stream and may fail with Stream consumed.
If middleware exhausts receive, a later request read can wait on an empty receive queue and block rather than producing an immediate error.
PR 1692 is a new candidate, but its creation event alone does not establish a stable implementation scope or adequate stream/disconnect tests.
The candidate must preserve downstream receive replacements and still needs explicit coverage for that flow and client disconnects.
The proposed ownership boundary is narrowed to body-buffer reuse for call_next inside BaseHTTPMiddleware rather than a general Request or scope cache.
The narrow proposal does not support endpoint-first consumption followed by middleware or exception-handler rereads; those would require information to flow upstream.
The proposal improves middleware-first body reads for the downstream endpoint but leaves other reread orders unsupported, so whether that narrow benefit is worth landing remains undecided.
The no-error hang remains reproducible after four years; full buffering can be an intentional HMAC tradeoff, but user-proposed scope and dummy-receive hacks are not production-ready repository fixes.
The proposed Request stream state machine lacks a standalone multi-chunk test and may mark the stream consumed before more_body becomes false.
Marking a Request stream consumed as soon as stream() starts or after its first yielded chunk is invalid for interleaved multi-chunk consumers.
The author confirms the multi-chunk concern exposed a real bug, reports reworking the implementation, and adds substantially more tests.
A maintainer formally approves the corrected final head and its expanded tests, resolving the repository decision about landing the narrow benefit.
PR 1692 merges as commit 554b9e2 and delivers the BaseHTTPMiddleware call_next body-buffer path plus request-stream and middleware regression tests.
Issue 495 closes after the merge, but closure applies to the delivered middleware-first target and does not make endpoint-first or exception-handler rereads supported.
How middleware can obtain routing information remains open.
Routing normally occurs after middleware executes.
Moving all middleware after routing is not the preferred default direction.
Endpoint response-time metrics need the matched route after the response without requiring endpoint instrumentation.
Per-Route or per-Mount middleware is a candidate way to avoid separate route matching.
PR #1286 is the active route-level middleware implementation attempt.
An application-level path_prefix option is proposed as an alternative.
The underdefined path_prefix proposal risks argument conflicts and reimplementing routing.
The active design investigation shifts from PR #1286 toward PR #1464.
PR #1286 closed without merge and is no longer an active implementation.
PR #1649 is an active attempt to add middleware to Mount.
Local middleware must not silently replace centralized application error handling and I/O.
The earlier PR #1464 direction was rejected rather than becoming the accepted solution.
Issue #685 has a closed tracker state at this cutoff; the event does not prove semantic resolution.
Per-Mount middleware does not by itself satisfy the original global route-name and APM use case.
The original global middleware requirement is disputed again and remains unresolved.
Low-touch APM cannot require users to attach middleware separately to every route or Mount.
Startup wrapping, monkeypatching, or a global route-middleware registry remain workaround directions while a framework feature is considered.
PR #2349 is a new per-route middleware implementation attempt, not yet proof that the global APM need is solved.
